Indian Geography - Consolidated Revision: Drainage System of India

What this is: a single revision file for India's drainage system, built from the class notes of 8, 9, 10, 12 and 21 September and 12 November 2026. Like the landforms revision file, each system has the map first, then the theory, then river-by-river details, important points and current affairs (to 15 November 2026).

Source class notes: 8 Sep (drainage concepts and patterns) | 9 Sep (Indus, IWT, Ganga basin) | 10 Sep (Ganga headwaters, tributaries, Kosi) | 12 Sep (Ganga floods, ILR, Son, Damodar, Brahmaputra) | 21 Sep (Brahmaputra tributaries, Teesta, Barak, east-flowing rivers) | 12 Nov (west-flowing and inland rivers)

Labels: [Current Affairs] boxes (blue) give dated developments with sources; [Important] boxes (purple) list the most-tested points; [Verification Required] flags figures that sources disagree on; † marks a standard textbook fact not re-checked against a page opened for this file. All maps are schematic: drawn on simplified Natural Earth data with hand-drawn, generalised river courses, approximate positions, not to scale and not Survey of India maps.
Contents: 1 Big picture | 1.4 Origins: glaciers, mountains, plateaus, dams | 2 Indus | 3 Ganga | 4 Brahmaputra and Barak | 5 East-flowing Peninsular | 6 West-flowing and inland | 7 Interlinking | 8 Water disputes | 9 Current-affairs table | 10 Mains themes | Key Facts | PYQs

1. The Big Picture: How India Drains, and Where Rivers Begin

1.1 Theory: basic terms

  • Drainage = the flow of water through well-defined channels; a drainage system = a river with its tributaries; a drainage basin (catchment) = the area drained by it; a water divide (watershed) = the high ground separating two basins (in planning, "watershed" also means a small catchment).
  • India's main divides: the Himalaya (Indus-Ganga-Brahmaputra vs Tibet), the Delhi Ridge-Aravalli (Indus vs Ganga), the Western Ghats (Bay of Bengal vs Arabian Sea) and the Vindhya-Satpura-Amarkantak highlands (Ganga vs Narmada-Mahanadi-Godavari).
  • About 77% of India's drainage area goes to the Bay of Bengal and about 23% to the Arabian Sea† (NCERT); a small part (Luni, Ghaggar) is inland.
  • The Ganga has India's largest basin (about 26.3% of the country).

1.2 Theory: why the two great systems differ

FeatureHimalayan riversPeninsular rivers
Source and flowGlaciers + rain: perennialRain only: seasonal (low flow in summer)
Age and stageYoung, still eroding: deep gorges, V-shaped valleysOld, mature: broad, shallow valleys; graded profiles
Course in plainsMeanders, braids, frequent course change (Kosi)Fixed courses in hard rock; few meanders
MouthHuge deltas (Ganga-Brahmaputra)East: deltas; West: estuaries
Basin and lengthVery large basins, long coursesSmaller basins; Narmada and Tapi are long exceptions in the west
UseIrrigation canals, navigation, hydropowerTank and dam irrigation, hydropower at falls

1.3 Theory: how the systems evolved

  • Antecedent rivers: the Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra (Dihang) are older than the Himalaya. As the ranges rose across them, they kept cutting down and made deep gorges (Figure 1, last panel). Consequent rivers follow the original slope; superimposed rivers inherit a course from an eroded cover rock (some Peninsular rivers, e.g. Damodar, Subarnarekha†).
  • Indo-Brahma (Shiwalik) hypothesis: a single great river may once have flowed north-west along the Himalayan front from Assam to Punjab; uplift of the Potwar plateau and Delhi Ridge split it into today's Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems. It remains a hypothesis.
  • Peninsular slope: the subsidence of the western flank after the Gondwana break-up and the general tilt to the east explain why most big Peninsular rivers flow east; the Narmada and Tapi flow west because they follow rift valleys (faults).
[Important]
  • Radial: Amarkantak (Narmada, Son, Mahanadi), Chota Nagpur, Kathiawar; centripetal: Loktak, Sambhar; trellis: Himalayan longitudinal valleys, Singhbhum.
  • Not "all Himalayan rivers are antecedent and all Peninsular rivers superimposed": these describe particular rivers.
  • Peninsular rivers do have floods, meanders and deltas locally (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri deltas).

1.4 Origins: Glaciers, Mountains and Plateaus

Theory: Himalayan rivers begin at glaciers (snouts) or glacier-fed lakes, so they are perennial; many rise north of the Great Himalaya (Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra, Karnali) and cut through it in antecedent gorges. Peninsular rivers begin at springs and hill-top catchments on the Western Ghats or central plateaus, so they depend on the monsoon. A few high points act as origin hubs from which several rivers flow out radially (stars on Map 1).

2. The Indus System

2.1 Theory and course

  • Source: Tibet, in the Kailash-Manasarovar region (not the lake itself), as the Senge Zangbo / Singi Khamban. Total length about 2,880 km† (India's share about 1,114 km†).
  • Course: flows north-west between the Ladakh and Zaskar ranges past Leh, receives the Zanskar near Nimmu and the Shyok (with the Nubra, which drains Siachen) near Skardu; turns south around Nanga Parbat through a spectacular antecedent gorge, receives the Gilgit (with the Hunza), and enters the plains at Attock; ends in the Arabian Sea near Karachi.
  • Panjnad: the five Punjab rivers unite: Jhelum and Ravi join the Chenab; Beas joins the Sutlej at Harike; Chenab + Sutlej form the Panjnad, which joins the Indus near Mithankot.

Chenab (Asikni)Chandra + Bhaga meet at Tandi (Lahaul, HP)Largest Indus tributary by flow†; Salal, Baglihar, Dulhasti, Ratle, Pakal Dul (on the Marusudar), Kiru, Kwar, Sawalkot; Chenab rail bridge
Ravi (Parushni)Bara Bhangal, Kullu hills (HP)Chamba valley; Ranjit Sagar (Thein) dam; part of the J&K-Punjab and India-Pakistan border

2.2 The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), 1960

  • Signed at Karachi, 19 September 1960, by Nehru and Ayub Khan; World Bank brokered it†.
  • Eastern Rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) for India's unrestricted use; Western Rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) mainly for Pakistan, with India allowed limited domestic, agricultural and run-of-the-river hydropower use under design limits.
  • Dispute ladder: Permanent Indus Commission (questions) → Neutral Expert (differences) → ad hoc Court of Arbitration (disputes).
[Important]
  • Order of the Punjab rivers west to east: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej. Prelims 2021 asked which of Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi and Sutlej "joins the Indus direct": the accepted answer is the Sutlej (through the Panjnad).
  • Vedic names: Vitasta = Jhelum, Asikni = Chenab, Parushni = Ravi, Vipasha = Beas, Shutudri = Sutlej.
  • Nubra and Galwan feed the Shyok; Hunza feeds the Gilgit; the Jhelum flows through Wular, not Dal.
  • Western rivers = Pakistan; Eastern rivers = India.
[Current Affairs] Indus
  • 23 April 2025: after the Pahalgam terror attack (22 April, 26 killed), India placed the IWT "in abeyance" until Pakistan "credibly and irrevocably" abjures cross-border terrorism (India had sought renegotiation in 2023 and 2024).
  • 31 August 2026: the Court of Arbitration (chair Prof. Sean D. Murphy) held unanimously that India's grounds could not suspend the treaty, so it "remains in force", and restricted concreting of the Ratle dam above certain levels until 90 days after the Neutral Expert's final decision (expected July 2027) (PCA press release). India rejected the award, calling the Court illegally constituted, and said the abeyance stays (MEA). An earlier pondage award (15 May 2026) was also rejected.
  • Chenab build-out: NHPC invited bids for the Sawalkot project (1,856 MW, two stages) in February 2026 (CNBC-TV18); sediment flushing has begun at Salal and Dulhasti-II (260 MW) got environmental clearance (BusinessLine). [Verification Required: commissioning targets for Pakal Dul, Kiru and Kwar come from media reports, not official releases.]
  • Exam angle (Mains 2016, 2026): water as both an asset and a source of conflict; treaty law vs security; storage on western rivers.

3. The Ganga System

3.1 Theory and course

  • Headstreams: the Bhagirathi (from Gaumukh, Gangotri glacier) and the Alaknanda (from Satopanth-Bhagirath Kharak glaciers, past Badrinath) meet at Devprayag; from there it is the Ganga. The Bhagirathi has naming primacy; the Alaknanda is the longer headstream.
  • Course: enters the plains at Haridwar; flows south-east past Kanpur, Prayagraj (Yamuna joins), Varanasi, Patna and Bhagalpur; at Farakka it splits: the main channel enters Bangladesh as the Padma, joins the Jamuna (Brahmaputra) and then the Meghna; the Bhagirathi-Hooghly distributary flows past Kolkata.
  • About 2,525 km long; basin about 26.3% of India; states: Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand (touch), West Bengal. National River (2008); NW-1 (Prayagraj-Haldia).
  • The Ganga is dendritic in the plains; it carries one of the world's largest sediment loads, building the Sundarbans delta.

  • Ghaggar is not Ghaghara; Jamuna (Bangladesh) is not Yamuna; Kali Gandaki (Gandak) is not Kali/Sharda (Ghaghara).
  • Kanwar (Kabar) Tal, Begusarai, is a Ramsar oxbow/floodplain wetland.
[Current Affairs] Ganga
  • Ganga Water Treaty with Bangladesh (1996, 30 years) expires on 12 December 2026. Renewal is uncertain; Bangladesh's BNP government seeks a "minimum guarantee" clause like the 1977 agreement; the Joint Rivers Commission met in Kolkata in March 2026 (Economic Times, 31 Oct 2026). Sharing at Farakka in the lean season (1 Jan-31 May): at 70,000 cusecs or less, 50:50; 70,000-75,000, Bangladesh gets 35,000; 75,000 or more, India gets 40,000 (ET Infra).
  • Namami Gange: 524 projects sanctioned, 355 (68%) completed by February 2026; India's first Dolphin Rescue Ambulance launched 13 January 2026 (PIB).
  • First riverine dolphin estimate (3 March 2025): 6,327 dolphins across 28 rivers in 8 States (6,324 Ganges river dolphins + 3 Indus river dolphins); UP 2,397, Bihar 2,220 (PIB).
  • Sone water MoU (31 August 2026): Bihar 5.75 MAF, Jharkhand 2 MAF (PIB).
  • Kishau dam agreement (15 September 2026): six States signed for a 232.6 m dam on the Tons with 1,562 MCM storage (PIB). A Rajasthan-Haryana Yamuna water project (29 June 2026) will carry about 580 MCM to Rajasthan by pipeline (PIB).
  • Yamuna at Delhi reached 207.48 m on 4 September 2025, third-highest since 1963 (record 208.66 m, July 2023).

4. The Brahmaputra and Barak Systems

4.1 Theory and course

  • Source: the Chemayungdung glacier near Manasarovar, Tibet; flows east as the Yarlung Tsangpo for about 1,200 km† along the Indus-Tsangpo suture, then makes a hairpin Great Bend around Namcha Barwa (eastern syntaxis) through one of the world's deepest gorges.
  • Enters Arunachal as the Siang / Dihang (antecedent gorge); near Sadiya it receives the Dibang and Lohit and becomes the Brahmaputra; flows west through the narrow Assam valley, then south into Bangladesh as the Jamuna, joins the Padma (Ganga) and then the Meghna.
  • Total length about 2,900 km†; basin shared by four countries (China, India, Bhutan, Bangladesh); main stem crosses three.
  • Character: very high discharge and sediment, braided channels and river islands (Majuli, the world's largest inhabited river island†; Umananda); severe annual floods and bank erosion in Assam.
BankTributaries (east to west)Notes
North (right)Dibang, Lohit (at Sadiya), Subansiri, Jia Bharali (Kameng), Manas, Sankosh, TeestaSubansiri: largest tributary; Lower Subansiri project (2,000 MW). Manas from Bhutan (Manas NP). Teesta: Sikkim-West Bengal-Bangladesh; joins the Jamuna; changed course in 1787
South (left)Burhi Dihing, Disang, Dikhow, Dhansiri, KopiliDhansiri drains Nagaland; Kopili from the Meghalaya-Karbi uplands

4.2 The Barak-Meghna

  • The Barak rises in the Manipur hills, loops past Tipaimukh, flows through the Barak valley (Silchar), and in Bangladesh splits into the Surma and Kushiyara, which reunite as the Meghna.
  • The Umngot at Dawki (Meghalaya), famous for its clear water, flows into Bangladesh (Dawki is the town, not the river).
[Important]
  • Names: Yarlung Tsangpo (Tibet) → Siang/Dihang (Arunachal) → Brahmaputra (Assam) → Jamuna (Bangladesh) → Padma + Meghna.
  • Jia Bharali = Kameng; Teesta is a right-bank tributary that flows south, not a west-flowing river.
  • Barak → Surma/Kushiyara → Meghna; the Sundarbans lie within the larger Bengal delta.
[Current Affairs] Brahmaputra and Teesta
  • Medog (Motuo) project, China: construction began 19 July 2025 at the Great Bend (five cascade stations, about 1.2 trillion yuan, reported ~60 GW): concerns over lean-season flows, sudden releases, sediment and seismic risk.
  • Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (India, ~11,200 MW): proposed as a buffer storage; as of 2 November 2026 only a pre-feasibility report is being prepared and there is no construction approval; local anti-dam protests turned violent in October 2026 (India Today).
  • Teesta: Bangladesh and China agreed (June 2026) to a feasibility study for the Teesta River Comprehensive Management and Restoration Project, a concern for India because it is close to the Siliguri Corridor; the India-Bangladesh Teesta sharing deal remains unsigned†.
  • Assam floods 2026: Charaideo received 436% above-normal rain on 18-19 July. [Verification Required: death tolls vary by source.]

5. East-Flowing Peninsular Rivers

5.1 Theory

  • Most rise in the Western Ghats or central highlands and flow east across the tilted plateau, cutting through the discontinuous Eastern Ghats, and build deltas on the broad east coast (gentle slope, heavy load, low tidal energy in the Bay).
  • Seasonal, rain-fed flow; deep, broad valleys; waterfalls where they cross scarps (Hundru, Chitrakote, Shivanasamudra, Hogenakkal); used for tank and canal irrigation since ancient times (Kallanai / Grand Anicut).

[Important]
  • Godavari tributaries (Prelims 2015): Indravati and Pranahita yes; Vamsadhara and Pennar no.
  • Eastern Ghats rivers (Prelims 2021): Nagavali and Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats; Brahmani and Subarnarekha rise on the Chota Nagpur plateau.
  • Chitrakote (Indravati) is not Chitrakoot; Kallanai is an anicut, Shivanasamudra a hydro station, Mettur a storage dam.
  • Kaveri gets both SW and NE monsoon rain: least seasonal of the Peninsular rivers.
[Current Affairs] East-flowing rivers
  • Mahanadi dispute (Odisha-Chhattisgarh): tribunal tenure extended to 13 January 2027; an expanded technical committee under the CWC chairman first met on 29 July 2026 to find a negotiated settlement (PIB).
  • Krishna (KWDT-II): tribunal must report by 31 July 2027; ad hoc sharing Telangana 299 tmc ft, AP 512 tmc ft (Deccan Chronicle).
  • Godavari-Banakacherla (Polavaram-Nallamala Sagar) link: Telangana's challenge to AP's plan to divert about 200 TMC; on 13 July 2026 the Supreme Court refused interim relief and asked Telangana to cure defects in its suit (Hindustan Times).
  • Polavaram: 90.1% physical progress (September 2026); diaphragm wall completed 2 April 2026 (New Indian Express).
  • Mekedatu (Kaveri): the Supreme Court dismissed Tamil Nadu's challenge (13 November 2025) as premature since only DPR preparation was allowed, and rejected its review petition on 21 May 2026 (New Indian Express).

6. West-Flowing and Inland Rivers

6.1 Theory

  • Narmada and Tapi flow west in rift valleys (grabens) between fault-bounded blocks (Vindhya-Satpura; Satpura-Satmala/Ajanta), so they keep a straight course against the general eastward tilt.
  • The short Western Ghats rivers are steep, fast and short, flowing over hard rock with little sediment; the coast is narrow and subsided, with strong tides and currents, so they form estuaries, not deltas (Mains 2013). Estuaries give brackish-water fisheries, mangroves and natural harbours.
  • Inland drainage: in the arid north-west, rivers such as the Luni and Ghaggar lose water by evaporation and seepage and never reach the sea; salt lakes (Sambhar, Didwana) collect centripetal drainage.
RiverSource / lengthKey points
NarmadaAmarkantak (Anuppur, MP); 1,312 km; largest west-flowing riverKapildhara and Dhuandhar falls, marble rocks at Bhedaghat (Jabalpur); Indira Sagar (India's largest reservoir by gross storage, 12.22 BCM), Omkareshwar (floating solar), Maheshwar, Sardar Sarovar (163 m, 2017; Statue of Unity); MP-Maharashtra-Gujarat; estuary near Bharuch; Narmada canal to Rajasthan

[Important]
  • Narmada flows west because of the rift valley (Prelims 2013); it touches Maharashtra only as a boundary.
  • Jog Falls is on the Sharavathi, not the Netravati; Dhuandhar is near Jabalpur, not Malwa (Prelims 2024).
  • Mullaperiyar: in Kerala, operated by Tamil Nadu; the dispute is over the water level (136 vs 142 ft) and safety.
  • Luni's "Saraswati" and "Sabarmati" branches are not the Gujarat Sabarmati or the Vedic Saraswati.
[Current Affairs] West-flowing rivers
  • Narmada (7 July 2026): MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Rajasthan signed a one-time settlement of outstanding dues under the 1979 Narmada tribunal award (Indian Express).
  • Mahi Banswara nuclear project (4 x 700 MW): foundation stone 25 September 2025 (12 Nov note).

7. Interlinking of Rivers (ILR)

  • National Perspective Plan (NPP), 1980: 30 links: 14 Himalayan + 16 Peninsular; run by the National Water Development Agency (NWDA). Envisaged benefits include about 34 GW of hydropower potential (not installed).
  • Logic: move water from "surplus" to "deficit" basins; flood moderation; irrigation; navigation (Mains 2020).
  • Concerns: doubtful "surplus" estimates, submergence of forests and wildlife habitat, displacement, sediment loss to deltas, high energy costs for lifting, inter-State disputes, climate uncertainty.

Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal-ERCP ("Ram Jal Setu", MP-Rajasthan)MoU January 2024, MoA December 2024; Chambal aqueduct under construction (target June 2028)Eastern Rajasthan drinking water and irrigation

8. Water Disputes: Inter-State and Transboundary

Key Facts for Prelims

  • Drainage share: ~77% to the Bay of Bengal, ~23% to the Arabian Sea†; Ganga basin largest (~26.3% of India).
  • Indus: Tibet (Kailash-Manasarovar region); Zanskar at Nimmu; Shyok (Nubra) near Skardu; Gilgit (Hunza); Panjnad at Mithankot. Punjab rivers W-E: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej.
  • IWT 1960: Western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan; Eastern (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India; in abeyance since 23 April 2025.
  • Ganga: Bhagirathi + Alaknanda at Devprayag; 2,525 km; Panch Prayag order Vishnu-Nanda-Karna-Rudra-Deva; Farakka → Padma + Hooghly.
  • Brahmaputra: Tsangpo → Siang/Dihang → (Dibang + Lohit at Sadiya) Brahmaputra → Jamuna; Majuli; Subansiri largest tributary.
  • Peninsular east: Godavari 1,465 km (Trimbakeshwar), Krishna ~1,400 km (Mahabaleshwar), Kaveri ~800 km (Talakaveri), Mahanadi (Sihawa; Hirakud 1957).
  • West-flowing: Narmada 1,312 km (Amarkantak), Tapi 724 km (Multai), Mahi crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice; Periyar is Kerala's longest.
  • Waterfalls: Dhuandhar (Narmada), Hundru (Subarnarekha), Chitrakote (Indravati), Jog (Sharavathi), Dudhsagar (Mandovi), Shivanasamudra and Hogenakkal (Kaveri).
  • Lakes: Wular (Jhelum), Kolleru (between Godavari and Krishna deltas), Kanwar (Bihar, oxbow), Loktak (centripetal), Sambhar (inland).
  • Glacier sources: Gangotri (Bhagirathi), Satopanth (Alaknanda), Yamunotri/Bandarpunch (Yamuna), Bara Shigri (Chandra), Siachen (Nubra), Rimo (Shyok), Zemu (Teesta), Milam (Goriganga), Chemayungdung (Brahmaputra); Rakas Tal (Sutlej), Beas Kund (Beas), Verinag (Jhelum).
  • Origin mountains/plateaus: Maikal (Narmada, Son), Satpura (Tapi), Western Ghats (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri), Chota Nagpur (Damodar, Subarnarekha), Vindhya (Chambal, Mahi), Aravalli (Luni, Sabarmati), Nandi hills (Pennar).
  • Dams: Tehri (Bhagirathi, highest), Bhakra (Sutlej), Indira Sagar (largest reservoir), Hirakud (Mahanadi), Sardar Sarovar (Narmada), Mettur (Kaveri).

Mains Points

  • Himalayan vs Peninsular rivers: perennial vs seasonal, young vs mature, deltas vs estuaries (west), different irrigation and flood problems.
  • Water diplomacy: IWT (abeyance vs arbitration), Ganga treaty renewal, Teesta and the China factor, Brahmaputra data-sharing.
  • Federal water governance: tribunal delays (Krishna, Mahanadi), negotiated settlements (Narmada dues, Sone MoU, Kishau), Supreme Court role.
  • Rivers and climate: glacier retreat, extreme rain and floods, sediment changes, delta subsidence.

Common Traps / Confusions

  • Ghaggar ≠ Ghaghara; Jamuna ≠ Yamuna; Chitrakote ≠ Chitrakoot; Kali Gandaki ≠ Kali/Sharda.
  • The Indus does not rise from Lake Manasarovar itself; the Sutlej rises at Rakas Tal.
  • Nubra/Galwan feed the Shyok; Hunza feeds the Gilgit.
  • India has limited (not zero) rights on the western rivers.
  • Chambal, Betwa and Ken join the Yamuna; Damodar joins the Hooghly.
  • Tehri is on the Bhagirathi; Jog is on the Sharavathi.
  • Pranahita = Wardha + Wainganga (Penganga joins the Wardha).
  • Mullaperiyar dispute = water level and safety, not dam height.
  • Ghaggar = Saraswati is a hypothesis.
  • Ken-Betwa redistributes water; it does not create new water.

30-Second Revision

  • Himalayan: perennial, antecedent gorges, deltas. Indus (IWT in abeyance; CoA award 31 Aug 2026 rejected), Ganga (treaty expires 12 Dec 2026), Brahmaputra (Medog vs Siang Upper).
  • Peninsular east: Mahanadi-Godavari-Krishna-Kaveri deltas; disputes (Mahanadi, Krishna, Banakacherla, Mekedatu).
  • West: Narmada-Tapi rifts and estuaries; short fast Ghats rivers; inland Luni and Ghaggar.
  • ILR: 30 links (14+16); Ken-Betwa first; PKC-ERCP.

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Questions marked "near-exact" come from secondary PYQ compilations and were not checked against the original UPSC paper.

Prelims

  • 2013: The Narmada flows west while most large peninsular rivers flow east. Why? Answer: it occupies a linear rift valley.
  • 2015: Which are tributaries of the Godavari: Vamsadhara, Indravati, Pranahita, Pennar? Answer: Indravati and Pranahita.
  • 2019: Glacier-river pairs such as Bandarpunch-Yamuna and Bara Shigri-Chenab (near-exact).
  • 2021: Of Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi and Sutlej, which "joins the Indus direct"? Accepted answer: Sutlej.
  • 2021: Which of Brahmani, Nagavali, Subarnarekha and Vamsadhara rise in the Eastern Ghats? Answer: Nagavali and Vamsadhara.
  • 2022: Gandikota canyon is on which river? Answer: Pennar.
  • 2022: Reservoir-State pairs: Ghataprabha, Gandhi Sagar, Indira Sagar, Maithon (near-exact).
  • 2023: Lake-river pairs: Wular-Jhelum, Kolleru-Krishna, Kanwar-Gandak (near-exact). Wular-Jhelum is correct; Kolleru lies between the Godavari and Krishna deltas.
  • 2024: Himalayan rivers joining the Ganga downstream of Prayagraj, west to east. Answer: Gomti-Ghaghara-Gandak-Kosi.
  • 2024: Waterfall-river pairs: Dhuandhar-Narmada, Hundru-Subarnarekha, Gersoppa-Netravati (near-exact). Gersoppa is on the Sharavathi.
  • 2026: A river that is antecedent, flows through three countries, rises on the Tibetan plateau and forms no distributaries (near-exact). Provisional key: Sutlej.
  • 2026: Ancient-modern name pairs: Vitasta-Chenab, Asikni-Jhelum, Parushni-Ravi (near-exact). Only Parushni-Ravi is correct (Vitasta = Jhelum, Asikni = Chenab).

Mains (GS I unless stated)

  • 2013: There is no formation of deltas by rivers of the Western Ghats. Why?
  • 2013 (GS II): constitutional mechanisms to resolve inter-State water disputes (near-exact).
  • 2014: Bring out the relationship between the shrinking Himalayan glaciers and the symptoms of climate change in the Indian sub-continent.
  • 2016: Present an account of the Indus Water Treaty and examine its ecological, economic and political implications in the context of changing bilateral relations (near-exact).
  • 2017: Floods as a source of irrigation and all-weather inland navigation (near-exact).

Verification Flags and Notes on Sources

  • River lengths depend on the measurement convention; NCERT/CWC figures are used. Superlatives ("largest", "longest") need a stated metric.
  • Chenab project commissioning targets, Assam flood tolls and the Teesta deal status come from media reports.
  • No 2025-26 Mullaperiyar ruling or Tulbul status was found.
  • Facts carried from class notes keep the corrections made there.
